notes.h: Two kinds of isomerism (Higher Level only)
points: Isomers are compounds with the same molecular formula but different arrangements of atoms.

Structural isomers have the same molecular formula but different structural formulae, so the atoms are joined in a different order; butane and methylpropane (C₄H₁₀), and but-1-ene and but-2-ene (C₄H₈), are examples.
Geometric, or cis–trans, isomers have the same molecular formula and the same structural formula, so the atoms are joined in the same order, but the atoms are arranged differently in space.
If converting one isomer into the other would mean breaking bonds and joining atoms in a different order, they are structural isomers.
If the order of joining is the same and only the positions in space differ, they are geometric isomers.

notes.h: Cis–trans isomers of butene (Higher Level only)
points: Geometric isomerism arises in alkenes because there is no rotation about the C=C double bond, since rotation would break the π bond, so groups are fixed on one side or the other of the double bond.
Each carbon of the double bond must carry two different atoms or groups for geometric isomerism to occur.
In cis-but-2-ene the two CH₃ groups are on the same side of the double bond, and the two H atoms are on the same side.
In trans-but-2-ene the two CH₃ groups are on opposite sides of the double bond.

notes.h: Which alkenes show cis–trans isomerism (Higher Level only)
points: But-1-ene, CH₂=CHCH₂CH₃, has no cis–trans isomers, because one carbon of the double bond carries two identical H atoms.
Methylpropene, CH₂=C(CH₃)₂, has none, because both carbons of the double bond carry identical pairs of groups.
Butene, C₄H₈, therefore has four alkene isomers: but-1-ene, cis-but-2-ene, trans-but-2-ene and methylpropene.
Alkanes have no geometric isomers, because groups rotate freely about C–C single bonds.
Other alkenes up to C6 with two different groups on each double-bond carbon, e.g. pent-2-ene, hex-2-ene and hex-3-ene, have cis and trans forms.

In a 3D model of but-2-ene the double bond, made of two flexible links, cannot be twisted, so the cis model cannot be turned into the trans model without taking it apart; digital models show the same when rotated.
Diagram: cis-but-2-ene and trans-but-2-ene drawn flat with 120° angles, the CH₃ groups circled on the same and on opposite sides.

notes.h: Structural isomers and chemical properties (Higher Level only)
points: Structural isomers of the same family, such as butane and methylpropane, have very similar chemical properties, because they have the same types of bond.

Structural isomers in different families have different chemical properties: hex-1-ene and cyclohexane are both C₆H₁₂, but hex-1-ene, with its C=C bond, decolourises bromine water, and cyclohexane, which is saturated, does not.
cis- and trans-but-2-ene have almost the same chemical properties, with the same C=C bond, the same addition reactions and the same combustion: C₄H₈ + 6O₂ → 4CO₂ + 4H₂O.

notes.h: Structural isomers and boiling point (Higher Level only)
points: Branched structural isomers have lower boiling points than unbranched ones, e.g. butane, −1 °C, and methylpropane, −12 °C.
The more compact shape of the branched isomer gives less contact and weaker London dispersion forces (see “Explaining and predicting properties”).

notes.h: Cis and trans isomers: physical properties (Higher Level only)
points: cis-but-2-ene boils at 4 °C and trans-but-2-ene at 1 °C.

The cis molecule is slightly polar, because both CH₃ groups lie on one side, so it has dipole–dipole attractions as well as London forces; the symmetrical trans molecule is non-polar (see “Polarity and symmetry”).
The trans isomer has the higher melting point, −106 °C compared with −139 °C for cis, because its more symmetrical, straighter shape packs more closely in the solid.
Cis–trans isomerism matters in food: unsaturated fats in natural oils are mainly cis.
Trans fats are formed when vegetable oils are partly hydrogenated, and they raise the risk of heart disease.

keyTerms.definition: Compounds with the same molecular formula but different arrangements of atoms.
Isomers with the same molecular formula whose atoms are joined in a different order.
Isomers with the same order of joining whose atoms are arranged differently in space, because of restricted rotation about a double bond.
A geometric isomer in which the groups of interest lie on the same side of a double bond.
A geometric isomer in which the groups of interest lie on opposite sides of a double bond.
The attraction between the permanent positive and negative ends of neighbouring polar molecules.
The addition of hydrogen across a double bond, used to partly harden vegetable oils.
An unsaturated fat with trans double bonds, formed when vegetable oils are partly hydrogenated.

questions.prompt: Distinguish between structural isomerism and geometric isomerism, giving an example of each from the isomers of C₄H₈.
questions.model: Structural isomers have the same molecular formula, but their atoms are joined in a different order. An example is but-1-ene, CH₂=CHCH₂CH₃, and but-2-ene, CH₃CH=CHCH₃. Geometric isomers have the same molecular formula and the same order of joining, but a different arrangement of the atoms in space; this is possible because there is no rotation about the C=C double bond. An example is cis-but-2-ene, with both CH₃ groups on the same side of the double bond, and trans-but-2-ene, with the CH₃ groups on opposite sides.

questions.prompt: Draw cis-but-2-ene and trans-but-2-ene. Explain why but-2-ene has geometric isomers but but-1-ene does not, and why butane has none.
questions.model: cis-but-2-ene has both CH₃ groups on the same side of the C=C double bond; trans-but-2-ene has them on opposite sides, with one H and one CH₃ group on each carbon of the double bond. But-2-ene has geometric isomers because each carbon of its double bond carries two different groups, and rotation about the C=C bond is prevented. But-1-ene does not, because one carbon of its double bond carries two identical H atoms, so the two arrangements are the same molecule. Butane has none because it has no double bond, and its groups rotate freely about the C–C single bonds.

questions.prompt: Explain how isomerism can give rise to different properties, referring to (i) hex-1-ene and cyclohexane, (ii) cis- and trans-but-2-ene.
questions.model: (i) Hex-1-ene and cyclohexane are both C₆H₁₂ but are structural isomers in different families. Hex-1-ene has a C=C double bond and decolourises bromine water by addition; cyclohexane is saturated and does not decolourise bromine water. (ii) cis- and trans-but-2-ene have the same C=C bond and almost identical chemistry, but different physical properties. cis-but-2-ene boils at 4 °C and trans-but-2-ene at 1 °C, because the cis isomer is slightly polar and has dipole–dipole attractions, while the trans isomer is non-polar. The trans isomer melts at −106 °C, compared with −139 °C for cis, because its symmetrical shape packs more closely in the solid.
